rendered:
The coating that retained the most capacity was LLTO-2 (the highest-loading coating, the 2 mol.% coating[1]), at 86.2%[2], slightly above LLTO-0.5 at 85.5%[3], and far above LLTO-1 at 57.2%[4], after cycling at 0.5C[5]. Pristine NCM only retained 56.6% of its initial discharge capacity after 200 cycles[6]. So the best LLTO coating keeps a much larger share of its initial capacity than bare NCM. The paper gives the main reason as is the prevention of direct[7] contact between the cathode and the electrolyte, which suppresses unwanted side reactions.

On rate capability: the paper says the LLTO coatings improve it through high ionic conductivity of the coating and suppressed side reactions, but the highest-loading coating lowered it. The stated explanation is coating thickness: which may be due to the increase in the[8] thickness of the coating layer, resulting in the suppression of electron[9] transfer process during charge/discharge cycling[10]. The paper hedges this with "may be", and its EIS comparison covers only pristine NCM and LLTO-1, so the thickness mechanism for the highest-loading sample is not directly measured. The text also does not explain why LLTO-1 retained far less capacity than both LLTO-0.5 and LLTO-2.
